title: 論語 泰伯第八
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 8, 〈泰伯〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 8 of the Analects, 泰伯 Tàibó, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Taibo"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book opens and closes with the sage rulers of old: Taibo, who three times gave up the succession to Zhou so quietly that no one could praise him for it (8.1), Yao, Shun and Yu, who held the world without making it their own (8.18–8.19), the few great ministers of Shun and King Wu (8.20), and Yu, who ate and dressed poorly and spent his strength on the field channels (8.21). Between them come Master Zeng's last words — showing his disciples hands and feet kept unharmed (8.3), and the dying man's words that are good (8.4) — and his picture of the officer, broad and resolute, whose charge is heavy and whose road is far, laid down only at death (8.7); the Master's three stages of learning — roused by the Odes, standing firm by the rites, made complete by music (8.8); his saying that the people can be brought to go by it but not to know it (8.9); and his advice to keep out of a state in peril and hide when the Way does not prevail (8.13). Each numbered passage (8.1–8.21, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 8.4 the edition we follow misprints 地 for 也; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
泰伯，
其可謂至德也巳矣。
三以天下讓，
民無得而稱焉。」

morph.gloss: Taibo — eldest son of the Great King of Zhou
(and that is all) (巳, the edition's form of 已)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Taibo —
he can surely be called utmost virtue, and that is all.
Three times he yielded the world,
and the people found no way to praise him for it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Taibo's virtue surely deserves to be called the utmost. Three times he gave the world away, and the people never knew what to praise him for.”
sentences.n: The book is named 泰伯 from its first words; Zhu Xi's heading says only that it has twenty-one chapters (凡二十一章). 泰伯 Taibo was the eldest son of the Great King of Zhou (大王), with two younger brothers, Zhongyong 仲雍 and Jili 季歷. 其可謂… 'surely (he) can be called…': 其 at the head softens the judgement into 'surely'. 至德 'utmost virtue' — Zhu Xi: virtue at its utmost, to which nothing more could be added. 也巳矣 piles three final particles, 'and that is all, it is so': a judgement stated with full conviction (the same clause is said of King Wen's virtue in 8.20, and has the same English there); 巳 is the edition's form of 已 yǐ here (as at 5.26 and 6.28), and He Yan's text has it too. 以天下讓 'taking the world, yielded (it)'; 三 'three times' — Zhu Xi: 三讓 means a firm refusal (固遜), not a count. 無得而稱焉 'had no way to praise (him) for it': 焉 'for it'. Zhu Xi tells the story: Shang's Way was waning and Zhou growing strong; Jili had a son, Chang 昌, of sagely virtue, and the Great King came to mean to overthrow Shang; Taibo did not go along with this, the King wished to pass his place to Jili and so on to Chang, and Taibo, knowing it, fled with Zhongyong to the Jing Man tribes of the south. Jili inherited; Chang came to hold two parts in three of the realm — he is King Wen — and Chang's son Fa conquered Shang and had the realm — King Wu. With his virtue, at the turn from Shang to Zhou, Taibo could have had the lords at his court and held the realm; he cast it away, and effaced his tracks too, so that his yielding was hidden and left no trace to see — hence the people found nothing to praise. His heart, Zhu Xi says, was the heart of Boyi and Shuqi when they 'held the horse' (扣馬 — by tradition King Wu's, as he set out against Shang), but his position was harder; no wonder the Master sighed over him and praised him. (Taibo's not going along, he notes, is recorded in the Chunqiu commentary, 春秋傳.) He Yan's Wang Su: knowing that Chang would surely have the realm, Taibo three times yielded the world to Jili; the yielding was hidden, so no one could praise him, and that is why it was utmost virtue.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
恭而無禮則勞，
慎而無禮則葸，
勇而無禮則亂，
直而無禮則絞。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Courtesy that does not go by the rites wears a man out; care that does not go by the rites leaves him afraid of everything; courage that does not go by the rites makes trouble; and straightness that does not go by the rites cuts like a cord pulled too tight.”
sentences.n: Four lines of one build: a quality, 而 'but', 無禮 'without the rites', then 則 'then' and what it turns into. 葸 xǐ (Zhu Xi: 絲里反) is the look of fear; 絞 jiǎo (古卯反) is 'to twist tight', and Zhu Xi glosses it 急切 'pressing, sharp'; He Yan's Ma Rong: 絞刺 'stinging, cutting'. Zhu Xi: without the rites there is no measure and form (節文), hence the four faults. He Yan's commentary on 葸: careful without the rites to regulate it, one is forever afraid.

sentences.t:
君子篤於親，
則民興於仁；
故舊不遺，
則民不偷。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
old friends, associates of long standing

sentences.l:
When the gentleman is devoted to his kin,
the people rise to humaneness;
when old friends are not cast off,
the people do not grow cold.
sentences.i: When the gentleman above them is warm toward his own kin, the people are stirred to humaneness; when he does not forget old friends, the people do not grow cold toward one another.
sentences.n: Two conditions, each joined to its result by 則 'then', with no word for 'when'. 君子 here, Zhu Xi says, is 'the man in high place' (在上之人) — the ruler whose example the people follow. 篤 dǔ is 'solid, earnest'; 興 xīng 'to rise, be stirred' (Zhu Xi: 起也); 故舊 'old associates', those one has known long; 遺 yí 'to leave behind, forget'; 偷 tōu, usually 'to steal', here 'thin, mean' (Zhu Xi: 薄也; He Yan's Bao Xian likewise ends 不偷薄也). Zhu Xi quotes Zhang Zai: when the way of men knows what comes first and what after, courtesy does not wear one out, care does not cower, courage does not riot, straightness does not cut; the people are transformed and their virtue grows thick. He also quotes Wu 吳氏: from 君子 on should be a chapter of its own, and is Master Zeng's words; and adds his own judgement: this section does not connect with what goes before and is close in spirit to 1.9 (慎終追遠), so Wu is probably right. We keep it in 8.2, as Zhu Xi prints it. Bao Xian: if the ruler is generous to his kin and does not forget his old friends, the people are transformed and rise to humane and generous conduct.

sentences.t:
曾子有疾，
召門弟子曰：「
啓予足！
啓予手！《詩》云：『
戰戰兢兢，
如臨深淵，
如履薄冰。』
而今而後，
吾知免夫，
小子！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
deference to elders, a younger brother's duty (later written 悌)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Master Zeng was ill.
He called the disciples of his school and said: “Lay bare my feet!
Lay bare my hands! The Odes say:
‘Trembling and wary,
as if looking down into a deep pool,
as if treading on thin ice.’
Now, and from now on,
I know I have come through,
my young ones!”
sentences.i: When Master Zeng was ill, he called his disciples to him and said: “Draw back the covers from my feet, and from my hands. The Odes say: ‘In dread, on guard, as at the edge of a deep pool, as on ice that may break.’ From this day on I know I am safe from all that, my lads.”
sentences.n: 曾子 Master Zeng (Zeng Shen, 1.4). 召 zhào is 'to summon'; 門弟子 'the disciples of his gate', i.e. his school (弟子 in its sense of a master's disciples). 啓 qǐ is 'to open' (Zhu Xi: 開也; the edition's form of 啟); 予 yú 'my'. Zhu Xi: Master Zeng had always held that the body is received from one's parents and must not be harmed, so now he had the disciples open his coverlet and look. The lines are from the ode Xiaomin 小旻: 戰戰 is fear, 兢兢 caution — doubled words that describe, bound here like 申申 in 7.4; one is afraid of falling at the edge of a deep pool, afraid of breaking through on ice. 而今而後 'now and after': from this moment on. 免 'to escape, come through' — Zhu Xi: only at the point of death did he know he had escaped harm to his body. 夫 fú is an exclamation (Zhu Xi: 音扶). 小子 'young ones' are the disciples (Zhu Xi: 門人也); he calls to them again when he has finished, to press the lesson home. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: of the gentleman one says 'he ended', of the small man 'he died'; the gentleman counts keeping his body whole till death as finishing his task, so Master Zeng counted returning whole as 'coming through'. Yin Tun: 'whole did his parents bear him, whole should the son return'; Master Zeng had them uncover his hands and feet at the end for this reason — who could do it without having grasped the Way? Fan Zuyu: if the body must not be marred, how much less may one mar one's conduct and so disgrace one's parents? He Yan's Zheng Xuan says the same of the coverlet; Kong Anguo: he quotes the ode to liken himself — always careful, fearing harm; Zhou Shenglie: only today do I know I have escaped trouble and disaster; 小子 are the disciples, called so that they would hear and remember.

sentences.t:
曾子有疾，
孟敬子問之。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Meng Jingzi — Zhongsun Jie, a grandee of Lu

sentences.l:
Master Zeng was ill,
and Meng Jingzi asked after him.
sentences.i: Master Zeng was ill, and Meng Jingzi came to ask how he was.
sentences.n: 孟敬子 Meng Jingzi, Zhu Xi says, was a grandee of Lu of the Zhongsun (= Mengsun) house, personal name Jie 捷; 問之 is to ask about his illness. He Yan's Ma Rong: a grandee of Lu, of the Zhongsun.

sentences.t:
曾子言曰：「
鳥之將死，
其鳴也哀；
人之將死，
其言也善。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Master Zeng spoke up and said:
“A bird that is near its death —
its cry is sorrowful;
a man that is near his death —
what he says is good.”
sentences.i: Master Zeng spoke to him unasked: “When a bird is dying its call is full of grief; when a man is dying, what he says comes from the best in him.”
sentences.n: The print has 地, a misprint for 也, corrected here. Both collation witnesses (Ruan's 1816 text and He Yan's text) read 其鳴也哀, and the clause is built exactly like the next, 其言也善, where 也 marks the pause after the topic: 'its cry — sorrowful', 'his words — good'. 鳥之將死 'a bird's being about to die': 之 between subject and verb makes the clause a time phrase, 'when a bird is about to die'; 將 jiāng 'about to'. 言曰 — Zhu Xi: 言，自言也, he spoke of his own accord, not in answer. Zhu Xi: a bird fears death, so its cry is sad; a man at the end of his road goes back to the root, so his words are good. It is Master Zeng's self-effacing way of putting it: he wants Jingzi to recognize that what follows is good and to remember it. He Yan's Bao Xian: he wished to warn Jingzi — 'I am about to die; my words are good and can be used.'

sentences.t:
君子所貴乎道者三：
動容貌，
斯遠暴慢矣；
正顏色，
斯近信矣；
出辭氣，
斯遠鄙倍矣。
籩豆之事，
則有司存。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
his bearing and looks: the whole person
his countenance, the expression of his face
his words and tone of voice
the bamboo and wooden vessels of the rites
a wooden dish on a stem

sentences.l:
What the gentleman prizes in the Way is three things:
moving his bearing,
he thereby keeps harshness and insolence far off;
setting his countenance right,
he thereby comes close to good faith;
bringing out his words and tone,
he thereby keeps the crude and the unreasonable far off.
The business of the bamboo and wooden vessels —
for that there are officers in charge.
sentences.i: There are three things in the Way that a gentleman sets most store by: that in every movement of his body he is free of harshness and insolence; that the face he composes is close to what he truly is; and that when he speaks, his words and his voice are free of anything crude or unreasonable. The arranging of the ritual dishes is the business of the officers in charge of it.
sentences.n: Master Zeng's words run on from the last unit; the commentary has broken them. 所貴乎道者三 'what (he) prizes in the Way are three': 所 + verb makes 'what he prizes', 乎 is 'in' (= 於), and 者 closes the noun phrase. Then three lines of one build: verb + object, 斯 'thereupon, thereby', and the result, sealed by 矣. Zhu Xi: 貴 is 'to set weight on'; 容貌 speaks of the whole person; 暴 is coarse and fierce, 慢 unrestrained; 信 is 'true, real' — a face set right and close to the truth, not a put-on gravity (非色莊); 辭 is words, 氣 the voice; 鄙 'common, vulgar'; 倍 is 背 'to turn one's back on' (reason). He reads 遠 and 近 in the departing tone (遠近並去聲), the verbs 'to keep far off' and 'to come near'; modern practice reads the verb 遠 yuǎn like the adjective, and we give that. 籩 biān is a bamboo dish, 豆 a wooden one (Zhu Xi: 籩竹豆，豆木豆) — the vessels of the sacrifices, standing for the counted details of the rites; 有司 'there are officers', i.e. the officers in charge. Zhu Xi: the Way is present everywhere, but the gentleman sets his weight on these three, the essentials of cultivating oneself and the root of government, to be held and examined without lapse even in haste or in ruin (造次顛沛, 4.5); the vessels belong to the Way too, but their place is the officers' charge. He quotes Master Cheng: these three correct oneself and seek nothing outside, hence 'for the vessels there are officers'; and Yin Tun: what is nourished within shows without — Master Zeng took cultivating oneself as the root of government. He Yan's Zheng Xuan reads the line the other way: he takes this 'Way' to be the rites and the results to be in others — move with dignity, and others will not dare to be harsh or insolent to you; keep a grave face, and they will not dare deceive you; speak smoothly, and no ugly, perverse words will reach your ears. Bao Xian: Jingzi neglected the great and attended to the small, so Master Zeng warned him with this. Variant: He Yan's text reads 君子所貴道者三, without 乎; the sense is unchanged.

sentences.t:
曾子曰：「
以能問於不能，
以多問於寡；
有若無，
實若虚；
犯而不校，
昔者吾友嘗從事於斯矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “To have ability and still put questions to those who lack it; to know much and still ask those who know little; to have plenty and carry himself as though he had none, to be full and carry himself as though empty; to be wronged and never keep a score — there was a friend of mine, long ago, who worked at just these things.”
sentences.n: A run of phrases with no subject, each a way of acting, and the last line sums them up as 斯 'these'. 以能問於不能 'with ability, to ask of the unable': 以 'with, having', 問於 'to ask of'. 實 shí 'solid, full', against 虚 xū 'empty' (虚 is the edition's form). 校 jiào — Zhu Xi: 計校, to reckon up, keep accounts; He Yan's Bao Xian: 報也, to pay back — wronged, he does not retaliate. 昔者 'in former times'; 嘗 'once'; 從事於斯 'to follow the work of these things'. The friend, Zhu Xi agrees with Ma Rong, is Yan Yuan: his heart knew only that what is right has no end, and saw no gap between himself and others, so he could do this. Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: not to know that the surplus is in oneself and the lack in others, not to insist that gain must be one's own and loss another's — only one who is close to having no self can do it.

sentences.t:
曾子曰：「
可以託六尺之孤，
可以寄百里之命，
臨大節而不可奪也，
君子人與？
君子人也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
six chi tall: still a boy
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Master Zeng said: “One who can be entrusted with an orphan of six chi,
who can be given charge of the commands of a hundred li,
who, facing the great crisis, cannot be wrested away —
a gentleman, is he?
A gentleman he is.”
sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “A man you could trust with a fatherless young lord, a man you could leave in charge of a whole state, a man nothing could prise loose when life and death are at stake — would you call him a gentleman? That is just what he is.”
sentences.n: 可以託 'can be entrusted with': 可以 + verb is passive in sense here, 'one to whom … can be entrusted'. 託 tuō and 寄 jì both mean 'to put in someone's keeping'. 六尺之孤 'an orphan of six chi' (尺, a measure of length): a ruler's son who is still a boy — He Yan's Kong Anguo: 'a young lord' (幼少之君). 百里之命 'the commands of a hundred li', a state of that size — Zhu Xi: his talent is such that he could assist a young lord and act for him in the government of the state; Kong Anguo: to act for the lord in his government and orders. 臨大節而不可奪 — Zhu Xi: his integrity (節) holds even at the meeting of life and death and cannot be taken from him; He Yan's commentary: the great crisis is to keep the state safe and the altars of the land secure, and 奪 is 'to be toppled'. 與 yú is the question particle (Zhu Xi: 平聲): the line asks 'a gentleman, is he?' and answers with 也 'he is'. Zhu Xi: 與 is a word of doubt, 也 a word of decision; setting it as question and answer makes the certainty stand out. He quotes Master Cheng: with integrity like this, he may be called a gentleman.

sentences.t:
曾子曰：「
士不可以不𢎞毅，
任重而道遠。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Master Zeng said: “An officer must not fail to be broad and resolute:
his charge is heavy, and his road far.”
sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “A man who would serve must have breadth and staying power, for what he takes on is a heavy weight, and the way he must carry it is far.”
sentences.n: 士 shì, the officer, the man of service who aims at the Way (as 4.9). 不可以不 'cannot do without being' — two negatives make 'must'. 𢎞 hóng is the edition's form of 弘 (He Yan's text writes 弘). Zhu Xi: 𢎞 is broad and wide (寬廣), 毅 strong and enduring (强忍); without breadth he cannot carry the weight, without resolve he cannot reach the end of the road. He Yan's Bao Xian: 弘 'great', 毅 'strong and able to decide'; only so can a man shoulder a heavy charge and go a long road. 任 rèn is 'a load, a charge'; 重 zhòng 'heavy'; 道 dào here is the road itself.

sentences.t:
仁以為己任，
不亦重乎？
死而後已，
不亦遠乎？
sentences.l:
Humaneness he takes as his own charge —
is that not heavy indeed?
Dying, and only then leaving off —
is that not far indeed?
sentences.i: Humaneness is the load he has taken on as his own — what could weigh more? He may set it down only when he dies — what road could be longer?
sentences.n: Master Zeng's words run on; the commentary has broken them. 仁以為己任 is 以仁為己任 'to take humaneness as one's own charge', with the object 仁 brought to the front for weight; 為 wéi 'to count as'. 不亦…乎 'is it not indeed…?' (1.1). 死而後已 'die and only then leave off'. Zhu Xi: humaneness is the whole virtue of the human heart, and to insist on embodying it in one's own person and practising it with all one's strength — that is heavy; while a single breath remains this resolve allows no slackening — that is far. He quotes Master Cheng: broad but not resolute, a man has no rule and can hardly stand; resolute but not broad, he is cramped and mean and has no room to dwell in it; and again: be broad and great, then resolute, and one can bear the heavy charge and reach far. He Yan's Kong Anguo: taking humaneness as one's charge, no charge is heavier; stopping only at death, no road is longer.

sentences.t:
子曰：
興於《詩》，
sentences.l: The Master said: One is roused by the Odes,
sentences.i: The Master said: A man is stirred to life by the Odes,
sentences.n: Three clauses of one build, verb + 於 'by, in' + the source; Zhu Xi interrupts after each and reads them as the stages of a learner's whole life. 興 xīng is 'to rise, be stirred' (Zhu Xi: 起也; He Yan's Bao Xian the same). Zhu Xi: the Odes are rooted in men's nature and feelings, some crooked and some straight; their words are easy to understand, and chanting them, with their rise and fall and repetition, moves people and easily goes in; so it is in the Odes that the beginner is stirred to love the good and hate the bad and cannot stop himself. Bao Xian: in cultivating oneself one should first study the Odes.

sentences.t: 立於禮，
sentences.l: stands firm by the rites,
sentences.i: steadied on his feet by the rites,
sentences.n: 立 'to stand, to be established' (as 2.4 三十而立). Zhu Xi: the rites have courtesy, reverence and yielding as their root and a full array of measure, form and number; they can bind fast the joints of a man's flesh and the sinews of his frame; so it is in the rites that the learner, midway, comes to stand on his own and not be shaken or swept off by things. He Yan's Bao Xian: the rites are that by which one stands.

sentences.t: 成於樂。
sentences.l: and is made complete by music.
sentences.i: and made whole by music.
sentences.n: 樂 here is yuè, 'music'. Zhu Xi: music has the five notes and twelve pitch-pipes, singing in turn and answering one another, to give the measure of song and dance on the eight kinds of instrument; it can nourish a man's nature and feelings, wash away what is crooked and foul and melt the dregs; so it is in music that the learner, at the end, reaches the point where what is right is refined and humaneness ripe, and he is of himself in tune with the Way and virtue — learning completed. He notes that the Neize chapter of the Record of Rites has a boy learn the manners of the young at ten, music and the reciting of Odes at thirteen, and the rites only at twenty; so the three here are not the order of a child's first lessons but the order, ease and depth of what is gained over a lifetime of greater learning. He quotes Master Cheng: the world does not lack men of fine talent, but because the learning of the Way is not clear, it comes to nothing; the Odes of the ancients were like the songs of today, which even village children heard and understood, so they were roused — now even old masters cannot make out their meaning; the ancients had rites for everything, from sweeping and answering to capping, marriage, mourning and sacrifice — now all are ruined; ancient music nourished the ear with its sounds, the eye with its colours, the nature with its songs, the blood with its dances — now none of it is left; so in antiquity men were easily made, and now with difficulty. He Yan's Kong Anguo: music is that by which one's nature is completed.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
民可使由之，
不可使知之。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The people can be brought to go by it;
they cannot be brought to know it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “You can get the people to walk the road; you cannot get them to see why it runs where it does.”
sentences.n: 可使 'can be made to': 使 is 'to cause'; 之 'it' is the Way, the right course. 由 is 'to go by, to follow' (He Yan's commentary: 用也, 'to use'). Zhu Xi: the people can be made to follow what principle makes right, but not made to know why it is so. He quotes Master Cheng: it is not that the sage does not wish every house to understand and every door to be enlightened; he simply cannot make them know, only make them follow. To say that the sage would not let the people know would turn it into the trick of 'four in the morning and three at night' (the monkey-keeper's ruse in the Zhuangzi) — how could that be the sage's heart? 可 is 'can', then, not 'may'. He Yan's commentary: they can be made to use it but not to know it — the common people use it every day and do not know it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
好勇疾貧，
亂也。
人而不仁，
疾之已甚，
亂也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Loving courage and chafing at poverty —
that makes for disorder.
A man who is not humane:
hate him too much,
and that makes for disorder.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A love of daring that cannot bear being poor ends in trouble. Hate a man who lacks humaneness too fiercely, and that too ends in trouble.”
sentences.n: 好 is hào 'to love' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 疾 is 'to be sick of, to hate': first of one's own poverty, then 疾之 of the inhumane man. 人而不仁 'a man, and yet not humane' (as 3.3). 已 'too, excessively'; 已甚 'too much'. 亂也 'it is disorder', i.e. it leads to disorder. Zhu Xi: one who loves courage and is not content with his lot will surely rise in revolt; one who hates the inhumane man and leaves him no place to stand will surely bring revolt on; the two hearts differ, one bad and one good, but they breed disorder alike. He Yan's Bao Xian: a man who loves courage and is galled by his own poverty and low station will surely make disorder; Kong Anguo: hating him too much also drives him to disorder.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
如有周公之才之美，
使驕且吝，
其餘不足觀也已。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “If one had talents as fine as the Duke of Zhou's,
supposing he were arrogant and mean,
whatever else he had would not be worth a look — and that is all.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Give a man gifts as splendid as the Duke of Zhou's: if he is proud and tight-fisted, nothing else about him deserves a second look.”
sentences.n: 如 'if' opens the supposition and 使 'supposing, should it be that' repeats it before the fault: two conditions, then the verdict. 周公之才之美 is 'the fineness of the Duke of Zhou's talents' — the second 之 links 才 to 美, 'the fineness of'. 其餘 'the rest of him'; 不足觀 'not enough to be looked at'; 也已 'and that is all', closing the judgement. Zhu Xi: 才美 is the fineness of intelligence, ability and skill; 驕 is boastful pride (矜夸), 吝 meanness and grudging (鄙嗇). He quotes Master Cheng: this puts in the strongest terms how impossible pride and meanness are — one with the Duke of Zhou's virtue would have neither of himself, but one with only his talents, if proud and mean, is not worth a look; and again: pride is the qi overflowing, meanness the qi shrinking. Zhu Xi adds his own view: though they differ as overflowing and shrinking, the two always go together — pride is the branches and leaves of meanness, meanness the root of pride; he had tested it on everyone, and never found a man proud and not mean, or mean and not proud. He Yan's Kong Anguo only identifies the Duke of Zhou as Dan 旦. Variant: He Yan's text ends 不足觀也已矣, with a further particle.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
三年學，
不至於穀，
不易得也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Three years of learning
without coming round to a salary —
not easy to find.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man who can study for three years without his thoughts turning to an official's pay is not easily found.”
sentences.n: The first two clauses make a topic, 'three years' learning and not reaching a salary', and 不易得也 is the comment: 'not easy to find'. 穀 gǔ is grain, and so the grain an officer is paid — Zhu Xi: 穀，祿也 'stipend'. 易 is yì, 'easy' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). Zhu Xi suspects 至 'to reach' should be 志 'to set the mind on' (至疑當作志): one who studies long without seeking a stipend is hard to find. He quotes Yang Shi: even a worthy like Zizhang asked about seeking a salary (2.18); how much more those below him — so a man who learns for three years without turning to a stipend is rare indeed. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads the line quite differently: 穀 is 善 'the good', and the saying means that no one who studies three years fails to reach the good — said to encourage people to learn. Variant: He Yan's text ends 不易得也已.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
篤信好學，
守死善道。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Firm in trust, loving learning;
keeping to it till death, making the Way good.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Hold firmly to what you trust and love learning; keep to it until you die, and so bring your Way to its best.”
sentences.n: Two lines of four characters, each two verb–object pairs. 篤 dǔ 'thick, firm' (Zhu Xi: 厚而力也, 'thick and forceful'); 信 here is to trust, to believe in (the Way), not the 'good faith' of one's word; 好 is hào, 'to love'; 守死 'to hold fast to death'; 善道 'to make one's Way good'. Zhu Xi pairs them: without firm trust one cannot love learning, but firm trust without love of learning may trust what is not right; without holding fast to death one cannot make one's Way good, but holding fast to death without making the Way good is only dying in vain. Holding fast to death is the fruit of firm trust, making the Way good the work of loving learning.

sentences.t:
危邦不入，
亂邦不居。
天下有道則見，
無道則隱。
sentences.i: Do not go into a state in danger, and do not stay on in one in turmoil. When the world is on the Way, step out into public life; when it has strayed from it, keep out of sight.
sentences.n: The saying runs on from the line before. Each clause fronts its object: 'an imperilled state — not enter'. 有道 / 無道 'has / lacks the Way' as in 5.1 and 5.20. 見 is read xiàn, 'to show oneself, to come forward' (Zhu Xi: 賢遍反), against 隱 'to hide, withdraw'. Zhu Xi: a gentleman meeting danger gives his life, so one already serving in an imperilled state may not rightly leave it, but one outside it need not go in; a disordered state is not yet in danger, but its punishments, government and order are in confusion, so he keeps himself clean and goes. 天下 speaks of the whole age; when it lacks the Way he hides himself and does not appear — which only one who is firm in trust, loves learning, holds fast to death and makes the Way good can do. He Yan's Bao Xian: 'do not enter' speaks of a man first meaning to go there, 'do not dwell' of one now wanting to leave; a minister killing his lord or a son his father is disorder, and danger is the omen of disorder to come.

sentences.t:
邦有道，
貧且賤焉，恥也；
邦無道，
富且貴焉，恥也。
sentences.l:
When the state has the Way,
to be poor and lowly is shameful;
when the state lacks the Way,
to be rich and high in rank is shameful.
sentences.i: Where the state follows the Way, it is a disgrace to stay poor and obscure; where it has lost the Way, it is a disgrace to be rich and honoured.
sentences.n: Still the same saying. Two lines of one shape: a condition, then 'poor and lowly — shameful'. 且 'and also'; 焉 after the description is a final particle, a pause before the verdict; 恥也 '(this) is shame'. Zhu Xi: when the age is well ordered and a man has no Way he can put into practice, or when it is in disorder and he has no integrity he can keep, he is a mere run-of-the-mill nobody, not fit to be counted an officer (士) — shame of the worst kind. He quotes Chao Yuezhi: with learning and with firmness, clean in the rights of going and staying and clear in the line between taking office and keeping out of it — only then is a gentleman's virtue whole.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不在其位，
不謀其政。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Not being in the post,
one does not lay plans for its government.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If the office is not yours, leave the planning of its business alone.”
sentences.n: Two clauses of four characters; the first, with no marker, is the condition of the second. 其位 'the post', 其政 'its government' — the two 其 point to the same office. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: not to be in the post is not to be charged with its affairs; but if the ruler or a grandee asks, one tells him. He Yan's Kong Anguo: it means each should keep wholly to the duties of his own office. Variant: He Yan's text ends 不謀其政也, with a final particle. The saying recurs in Book 14, where Zhu Xi marks it 重出 'repeated'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
師摯之始，《關雎》之亂，
洋洋乎盈耳哉！」

morph.gloss: Music Master Zhi — the music master of Lu
the Guanju, the first of the Odes
the osprey (in the Ode 關雎)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “At the start of Music Master Zhi, the finale of the Guanju —
flowing full — brimming in the ears!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When Music Master Zhi was new in his post, the closing strains of the Guanju poured out wide and rich, more than the ear could hold!”
sentences.n: Two phrases with 之 'of' set the scene; then the exclamation 洋洋乎…哉. 師 is the title 'music master', 摯 zhì his name (Zhu Xi: 摯音志): Zhu Xi, the music master of Lu named Zhi. 亂 here is not 'disorder' but the closing section of a piece of music (樂之卒章); Zhu Xi cites the Shiji: 'the finale of the Guanju was made the beginning of the Airs'. 洋洋 'broad-flowing', for a sense of beauty and fullness (美盛意); doubling makes it describe a manner. Zhu Xi reads 師摯之始 as a time: when Confucius came back to Lu from Wei and set the music right, it happened to be early in Master Zhi's tenure, so the music was as fine as this. He Yan's Zheng Xuan reads it otherwise: 始 is 首 'first', and 亂 is real disorder — when the Zhou Way declined, the tunes of Zheng and Wei arose and the correct music lost its measure; Zhi, the Grand Music-Master (大師) of Lu, knew the sound of the Guanju and was the first to set its disorder right. 關雎 is the Odes' first poem (3.20).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
狂而不直，
侗而不愿，
悾悾而不信，
吾不知之矣。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Wild and yet crooked, dull and yet careless, empty-headed and yet false — what can I do with such men?”
sentences.n: Three lines of one shape, A 而不 B, 'A yet not B': each fault lacks the saving quality that usually goes with it. 狂 'wild, high-aiming' (5.21). 侗 'ignorant, unformed' (Zhu Xi: 無知貌); he reads it 音通, tōng, but modern practice reads this word tóng, which we give. 愿 yuàn 'careful and honest' (Zhu Xi: 謹厚也). 悾悾 kōng kōng (Zhu Xi: 音空) 'incapable-looking' (無能貌). 吾不知之矣 'I do not know them': Zhu Xi calls it a phrase of utter rejection — he would not even stoop to teach them. He quotes Su Shi: Heaven makes things with uneven endowments; below the middle grade, where there is a fault there is a matching virtue — the horse that kicks and bites is sure to run well, the one that cannot run is sure to be docile; to have the fault without the virtue makes one the world's waste material. He Yan's commentators: Kong Anguo, the wild should at least be straight, and 侗 is one not yet formed into a vessel, who ought at least to be careful; Bao Xian takes 悾悾 as 慤慤 'simple, plain', who ought at least to be trustworthy; Kong Anguo, all of these go against the normal measure, so 'I do not understand them'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
學如不及，
猶恐失之。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Learning as if never catching up,
still one fears to lose it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Study as if you were always falling behind, and even so be anxious that what you have may slip from you.”
sentences.n: 學如不及 'learn as though not reaching'; 猶 'still, even so'; 之 'it', what one is learning. Zhu Xi: when a man learns, he is already as if he could not reach it, and yet his heart still trembles lest he lose it — a warning that this is how a learner should be. He quotes Master Cheng: no letting anything slip past; the moment you say 'let it wait till tomorrow', it will not do. He Yan's commentary: learning comes in from outside and lasts only when it is ripe; so one is as if not reaching it, and still afraid of losing it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
巍巍乎！
舜禹之有天下也，
而不與焉。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Towering!
Shun and Yu's having the world —
and yet they had no part in it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Shun and Yu — how they tower! The whole world was theirs, yet they had no stake in it for themselves.”
sentences.n: 巍巍乎 'towering!' is an exclamation set first; then a topic made with 之 between subject and verb, 舜禹之有天下也 'Shun and Yu's possessing the world', and 而不與焉 'yet they did not take part in it'. 與 is read yù, 'to be concerned in, have a part in' (Zhu Xi: 去聲); he glosses 不與 as 不相關 'having nothing to do with it' — they did not take their high place as a thing to enjoy. 巍巍 'lofty and great' (Zhu Xi: 高大之貌). He Yan's commentary takes it differently: it praises Shun and Yu who did not themselves seek the realm (不與求), and yet got it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
大哉堯之為君也！
巍巍乎！
唯天為大，
唯堯則之。
蕩蕩乎！
民無能名焉。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “How great it was, Yao's being lord!
Towering!
Only Heaven is great,
and only Yao took it as his measure.
Broad and far-reaching!
The people had no means to name it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “How great Yao was as lord of men! So high — Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone made himself its match. So wide — there was nothing the people could call it by.”
sentences.n: 大哉 'how great!' comes first, and its subject follows: 堯之為君也 'Yao's being lord' (為 wéi, 之 making the clause a noun). 唯 'only' (Zhu Xi: 猶獨也). 為大 'is great' (為 wéi). 則 here is a verb, 'to match, to take as standard' (Zhu Xi: 猶準也); 蕩蕩 'broad and far-reaching' (廣遠之稱); 名 'to name' as a verb, 焉 'it'. Zhu Xi: of all things none is higher or greater than Heaven, and only Yao's virtue could match it; so its breadth, like Heaven's, could not be shaped in words. He Yan's Kong Anguo takes 則 as 法 'to model oneself on': Yao could model himself on Heaven in transforming the people; Bao Xian: 蕩蕩 is broad and far — his virtue spread so wide that the people could not know how to name it.

sentences.t:
巍巍乎其有成功也！
煥乎其有文章！

morph.gloss: patterns — the rites, music and laws
a finished pattern, a design (成章)

sentences.l:
Towering, his accomplished works!
Shining, his patterns!
sentences.i: How high his achievements stood! How brightly shone the rites, the music and the laws he gave!
sentences.n: The saying runs on. Two exclamations of one shape: a description with 乎, then the subject, 其有 X 'his having X'. 成功 'accomplished works' (Zhu Xi: 事業也); 煥 huàn 'bright, shining' (光明之貌); 文章 here is the rites and music, laws and measures (禮樂法度也). Zhu Xi: Yao's virtue could not be named; what could be seen of it was only this. He quotes Yin Tun: the Way of Heaven is great and accomplishes without acting; only Yao matched it in ruling the world, so the people could find nothing to name it by — what could be named was only his works and his patterns, towering and shining. He Yan's commentary: his work complete and his transforming influence high, he is 'towering'; 煥 is bright — the patterns he set up and the institutions he handed down were brilliant too. Variant: Ruan's 1816 text ends 其有文章也, with a final particle.

sentences.t:
舜有臣五人，
而天下治。
sentences.l:
Shun had ministers, five men,
and the world was in order.
sentences.i: Five ministers served Shun, and all the world was in good order.
sentences.n: 臣五人 'ministers, five men': the number follows the noun, with 人 as its counter. 而 'and so'. 治 zhì 'to be well ordered'; Zhu Xi marks it 去聲, the reading for 'in order' as against the level-tone 'to govern' — modern Mandarin reads both zhì. The five, Zhu Xi says (and He Yan's Kong Anguo the same), were Yu 禹, Ji 稷 (Lord Millet), Xie 契, Gao Yao 皋陶 and Bo Yi 伯益.

sentences.t:
武王曰：「
予有亂臣十人。」

morph.gloss: King Wu — founder of the Zhou dynasty

sentences.l: King Wu said: “I have ministers who bring order, ten men.”
sentences.i: King Wu said: “I have ten ministers to set the world in order.”
sentences.n: 予 is yú, 'I'. Zhu Xi: these are words from the 'Great Declaration' (泰誓) of the Documents. 亂 here means 'to put in order', the reverse of its usual sense — Zhu Xi cites Ma Rong: 亂，治也 (He Yan's Kong Anguo: 亂，理也), and records the view that the character was once 乿, an old form of 治. So 亂臣 are 'ministers who bring order', not rebels. The ten, Zhu Xi says, were Dan the Duke of Zhou, Shi the Duke of Shao, Taigong Wang, the Duke of Bi, the Duke of Rong, Tai Dian, Hong Yao, San Yisheng, Nangong Kuo — and one more, who was 'Wen's mother' (文母), King Wen's queen and King Wu's mother; this is Kong Anguo's reading too. Zhu Xi adds the objection of Academician Liu 劉侍讀: a son cannot make his own mother his subject, so she must be Yi Jiang 邑姜 (by tradition King Wu's queen) — nine ministers ordering affairs outside and Yi Jiang within.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
才難，
不其然乎？
唐虞之際，
於斯為盛。
有婦人焉，
九人而已。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said: “Talent is hard to find —
is it not indeed so?
The meeting of Tang and Yu
was more flourishing than this.
There was a woman among them:
nine men, and that is all.”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “They say talent is hard to find — and is it not so? Only the age when Yao handed the realm to Shun was richer in it than this. And one of these ten was a woman, so there were only nine men.”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi on why the record says 孔子 'Kongzi', not 子 'the Master': the words are joined to King Wu's, about a ruler and his ministers, and the recorder is being careful. 才難 'talent is hard (to come by)' is probably an old saying (蓋古語) which Confucius confirms with 不其然乎 'is it not so?' (難 nán). 才, Zhu Xi says, is virtue put to use. 唐 and 虞 were the dynastic names of Yao and Shun; 際 is their meeting, the time when one handed the realm to the other (交會之閒). 於斯為盛: 於 'than', 斯 'this', the Zhou; 為 wéi. Zhu Xi: for all the Zhou's wealth of talent, only the meeting of Tang and Yu was more flourishing than it, and from Xia and Shang down none could match it — yet even so there were only these few, which shows how hard talent is to find. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads the comparison the other way: set beside the meeting of Yao and Shun, the Zhou was the most flourishing and richest in worthy men — yet even it had one woman and nine others, no more. 婦人 'a woman' is the tenth of King Wu's ministers (see the line before).

sentences.t:
三分天下有其二，
以服事殷。
周之德，
其可謂至德也已矣。
sentences.l:
The world divided in three, he had two parts of it,
and with them served Yin in submission.
The virtue of Zhou —
it can surely be called utmost virtue, and that is all.
sentences.i: When two of the world's three parts were already his, he still used them to serve Yin as its subject. The virtue of Zhou surely deserves to be called the utmost.
sentences.n: 三分天下有其二 'dividing the world in three, he had two of its (parts)': 三 is adverbial 'in three', and 其二 'two of them'. The subject is King Wen, not named. 以 'with (them), thereby'; 服事 'to serve submissively'; 殷 Yin, the Shang. 其可謂至德也已矣 is the clause said of Taibo in 8.1, and has the same English: 其 'surely', 可謂 'can be called', and 也已矣 heaping up final particles for emphasis. Zhu Xi cites the Chunqiu commentary (春秋傳): King Wen led the states that had broken with Shang to serve Zhou 紂, its king; and he explains that six provinces (Jing, Liang, Yong, Yu, Xu, Yang) had turned to Wen, and only Qing, Yan and Ji still belonged to Zhou 紂. He quotes Fan Zuyu: Wen's virtue was enough to replace Shang, Heaven gave it him and the people turned to him, yet he did not take it but served — that is why it is utmost virtue. Zhu Xi: Confucius goes on from King Wu's words to King Wen's virtue, and calls it utmost virtue just as he did Taibo's; the point is a subtle one. He records too a view that the passage should be cut here, and 三分天下… made a chapter of its own, starting from 孔子曰. He Yan's Bao Xian: Zhou 紂 of Yin was dissolute; King Wen, as Lord of the West, had a sage's virtue, and two thirds of the world turned to him, yet he still served Yin — so it is called utmost virtue. Variant: He Yan's text reads 周德 without 之, the same sense.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
禹，吾無閒然矣。
菲飲食而致孝乎鬼神；
惡衣服而致美乎黻冕；
卑宫室而盡力乎溝洫。
禹，吾無閒然矣。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “In Yu I can find no chink to pick at. He kept his own food and drink scant, but spared nothing in what he offered the spirits; his everyday clothes were plain, but his apron and cap for the sacrifice were as fine as could be; he lived in a low house, but put all his strength into the ditches and channels of the fields. In Yu I can find no chink to pick at.”
sentences.n: The opening and closing line is the same: 禹 'as for Yu', then 吾無閒然矣 'I have no gap (to find) in him' — 閒 is the edition's form of 間, read jiàn, 'a crack, a gap' (Zhu Xi: 去聲; 閒，罅隙也): to point out a crack and find fault; 然 rounds the phrase off as a description. Between, three lines of one shape: A B 而致/盡 C 乎 D, 'sparing in A–B, yet giving C fully to D' — 乎 = 於 'to, on'. 菲 fěi 'thin, meagre' (Zhu Xi: 音匪, 薄也; He Yan's Ma Rong the same); 飲 yǐn, 食 shí. 致孝乎鬼神, Zhu Xi says, is making the sacrificial offerings rich and clean. 惡 è 'poor, coarse', as 4.9 惡衣; 衣服 everyday dress; 黻 fú (音弗) is the knee-cover, made of leather, and 冕 the ceremonial cap — both sacrificial dress. He Yan's Kong Anguo: he cut back his ordinary clothes to make his sacrificial clothes splendid. 卑 'low'; 宫室 'house and rooms' (宫 the edition's form of 宮). 溝洫 xù (呼域反) are the water channels between the fields, which marked the field boundaries and guarded against drought and flood (Zhu Xi); He Yan's Bao Xian gives the measures: a square li of fields is a 'well' (井), and between wells runs a 溝 four chi wide and deep; ten li make a 城, and between these runs a 洫 eight chi wide and deep. Zhu Xi: here lavish, there sparing, each as was fitting — so there was no crack to fault, and he says it twice to praise Yu deeply. He quotes Yang Shi: thin in what he gave himself, he spent his effort on the people's affairs and his adornment on the rites of temple and court — 'having the world and taking no part in it' (8.18); what gap could there be? He Yan's Kong Anguo: Confucius extols the greatness of Yu's merit and virtue — he could find no gap to put himself into. The passage closes Book 8.
